title: Self-Supervised Pretraining of Molecular Graph Encoders with LeJEPA
summary: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its value for molecular graph neural networks remains contested. We ask whether pretraining on a large unlabelled corpus improves molecular property prediction. We adapt LeJEPA, a predictor-free joint-embedding predictive architecture regularised by Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularisation (SIGReg), to molecular graphs, evaluating GPS and Chemprop-style D-MPNN encoders on the Wong et al. [1] antibiotic-activity dataset and ogbg-molhiv using a multi-seed, bootstrap-based protocol. Pretraining improves learned representations but does not robustly improve finetuning. A frozen probe on pretrained embeddings exceeds random initialisation on both tasks (ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC 0.788 vs 0.665; +0.123), reaching the published self-supervised band, but this does not translate into finetuning gains. On the antibiotic scaffold split, a canonical partition is significant (delta AUPRC +0.041, p = 0.010), but the effect vanishes across five partitions (pooled +0.013, p = 0.095). Finetuning is null on the random split, ogbg-molhiv, and D-MPNN. The representational edge is nevertheless recoverable. Embeddings saturate at ~16-32 effective dimensions, whereas Morgan fingerprints improve to 1024 bits. At matched dimensionality, fingerprints lead validation (0.799 vs 0.782 at 128 dimensions) but trail shifted test scaffolds (0.759 vs 0.788). Truncating embeddings and combining them with a 1024-bit Morgan fingerprint raises ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC from 0.805 to 0.832 (delta +0.027; 95% CI [+0.003, +0.054]; p = 0.014); an untrained encoder gains nothing (delta -0.003). Thus, pretraining supplies complementary information best realised through feature-level combination, while finetuning gains are weak and partition-dependent.

AI.tldr: Pretraining molecular graphs with LeJEPA/SIGReg improves learned representations but does not robustly improve finetuning. Pretrained embeddings outperform random initialisation on frozen probes and, when truncated and combined with Morgan fingerprints, boost ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC from 0.805 to 0.832. However, finetuning gains are weak, partition-dependent, and null across most splits and encoder settings.
AI.motivation: The value of self-supervised pretraining for molecular graph neural networks is contested despite its success in language and vision, motivating a rigorous evaluation of whether pretraining on large unlabelled molecular corpora actually improves downstream molecular property prediction.
AI.method: Adapts LeJEPA (a predictor-free joint-embedding predictive architecture with SIGReg regularisation) to molecular graphs. Evaluates GPS and Chemprop-style D-MPNN encoders on antibiotic-activity (Wong et al.) and ogbg-molhiv datasets using multi-seed bootstrap-based protocols, frozen probes, finetuning, dimensionality truncation, and feature-level combination with Morgan fingerprints.
AI.result: Frozen probe on pretrained embeddings beats random initialisation on both tasks (ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC 0.788 vs 0.665). Finetuning gains are null except one scaffold split (delta AUPRC +0.041, p=0.010) that vanishes across five partitions (pooled +0.013, p=0.095). Truncated embeddings combined with Morgan fingerprints raise ogbg-molhiv ROC-AUC from 0.805 to 0.832 (delta +0.027; p=0.014).
AI.conclusion: Pretraining supplies complementary molecular information best exploited via feature-level representation combination rather than finetuning. Finetuning benefits are weak and partition-dependent, while frozen embeddings combined with classical fingerprints provide robust gains.

title: MarkerScout: A Disease-Agnostic Machine Learning Framework for Biomarker Prediction from Multi-Scale Mechanistic Models
summary:
We demonstrate the framework on three infectious diseases derived from a companion mechanistic immune-simulation platform: SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A Virus, and Plasmodium falciparum. Each disease was evaluated across hospitalization and intensive care unit cohorts, yielding six cohorts in total. Best-pipeline cross-validated macro F1 ranged from 0.82 for IAV-HOSP to 0.99 for COV-ICU, and the framework produced tiered, direction-aware biomarker lists for each disease and phase. Interleukin-18 (IL-18) reached the strongest tier in both SARS-CoV-2 phases with consistent direction.
  When benchmarked against three separate, independently collected clinical ICU datasets, MarkerScout's top-ranked features outperformed 94.4% of randomly selected feature sets of equivalent size for SARS-CoV-2, with a weaker but directionally consistent advantage for Influenza A Virus (66.7%) and Plasmodium falciparum (60.7%).

AI.tldr: MarkerScout is a biomarker discovery framework demonstrated on three infectious diseases (SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A Virus, Plasmodium falciparum) across hospitalization and ICU cohorts. It achieves cross-validated macro F1 scores from 0.82 to 0.99 and produces tiered, direction-aware biomarker lists. When benchmarked against independent clinical ICU datasets, its top-ranked features outperform 94.4% of random feature sets for SARS-CoV-2, with weaker but directionally consistent advantages for IAV (66.7%) and Pf (60.7%). IL-18 emerged as a strong, consistently directed biomarker across SARS-CoV-2 phases.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to validate a biomarker discovery framework (MarkerScout) across multiple infectious diseases and clinical cohorts, demonstrating that machine-learning-driven feature selection can produce robust, direction-aware, and generalizable biomarkers validated against independent datasets.
AI.method: MarkerScout is applied to six cohorts derived from a companion mechanistic immune-simulation platform, covering three diseases (SARS-CoV-2, IAV, Plasmodium falciparum) across hospitalization and ICU settings. The framework produces tiered, direction-aware biomarker lists per disease/phase, and top-ranked features are benchmarked against three independently collected clinical ICU datasets using percentile-based comparison against random feature sets.
AI.result: Best-pipeline cross-validated macro F1 ranged from 0.82 (IAV-HOSP) to 0.99 (COV-ICU). IL-18 reached the strongest tier in both SARS-CoV-2 phases with consistent direction. Top-ranked features outperformed 94.4% of random feature sets for SARS-CoV-2 ICU, 66.7% for IAV, and 60.7% for Plasmodium falciparum in independent clinical benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: MarkerScout demonstrates strong performance and external validity for SARS-CoV-2 biomarker discovery, with directionally consistent but weaker generalization to Influenza A Virus and Plasmodium falciparum. IL-18 is identified as a robust, reproducible biomarker for SARS-CoV-2 across disease phases.

title: Towards AI-Driven Nanomedicine Discovery: A Benchmark and Multimodal Learning Framework for Nano Self-Assembly Prediction
summary: Nano self-assembly organizes molecular components into bioactive nanoscale structures. Self-assembled nanoparticles (NAPs) derived from Chinese herbal formulas and applications such as anti-lung-cancer therapy demonstrate the substantial potential of self-assembly for nanomedicine discovery. Yet discovery still relies on costly wet-lab screening, while existing machine learning approaches lack standardized tasks, effective pairwise compatibility modeling, and public benchmarks with unified evaluation. To address these limitations, we formalize NSA prediction as a binary classification task for predicting self-assembly between molecular pairs and then establish NSA-Bench, the first public benchmark with curated molecular combinations, experimental conditions, self-assembly labels, and standardized evaluation protocols. We further develop NSA-Net, an interaction-aware multimodal framework that integrates complementary molecular evidence from graph topology, sequence semantics, and physicochemical descriptors to learn molecular-pair representations for self-assembly prediction. Extensive experiments on NSA-Bench show that NSA-Net achieves a ROC-AUC of $0.9470\pm0.0112$ (Small) and $0.9492\pm0.0062$ (Large). On the Small track, it surpasses the strongest machine-learning and graph-based baselines by 3.9 and 17.1 percentage points, respectively. Representation analyses reveal interpretable molecular characteristics associated with self-assembly prediction captured by the learned representations. Moreover, an NSA-Agent case study further demonstrates how NSA-Net predictions can support formulation refinement through experimental-condition-aware reasoning. Our code is available at https://github.com/developer-hq/NSA-Net.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces NSA-Bench, the first public benchmark for nano self-assembly (NSA) prediction, formalized as a binary classification task between molecular pairs. The authors develop NSA-Net, an interaction-aware multimodal framework integrating graph topology, sequence semantics, and physicochemical descriptors, achieving ROC-AUC of 0.9470±0.0112 (Small) and 0.9492±0.0062 (Large), surpassing baselines by 3.9–17.1 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Nano self-assembly has great potential for nanomedicine discovery, but current discovery relies on costly wet-lab screening. Existing machine learning approaches lack standardized tasks, effective pairwise compatibility modeling, and public benchmarks with unified evaluation.
AI.method: Formalize NSA prediction as binary classification between molecular pairs; establish NSA-Bench (first public benchmark with curated molecular combinations, conditions, labels, and evaluation protocols); develop NSA-Net, a multimodal framework integrating graph topology, sequence semantics, and physicochemical descriptors for molecular-pair representation learning. Also build NSA-Agent for experimental-condition-aware reasoning in formulation refinement.
AI.result: NSA-Net achieves ROC-AUC of 0.9470±0.0112 (Small) and 0.9492±0.0062 (Large), outperforming the strongest ML and graph baselines by 3.9 and 17.1 percentage points respectively on the Small track. Representation analyses reveal interpretable molecular characteristics; NSA-Agent case study demonstrates formulation refinement support.
AI.conclusion: The work addresses a critical gap in NSA prediction by providing standardized benchmark and effective multimodal prediction framework, advancing computational approaches for nanomedicine discovery and reducing reliance on costly wet-lab screening.

title: Advancing Alzheimer's Disease Treatment: Synergistic Ligand Combinations Targeting BACE1 via Multi-Ligand Simultaneous Docking
comment: \c{opyright} 2025 by the Author(s). This article is an open access article distributed under the terms and conditions of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License
summary: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by memory loss, cognitive decline, and behavioral changes, primarily affecting the elderly. Current treatments focus on symptom management as no therapies effectively halt or reverse disease progression. Newer therapies targeting BACE1, a key enzyme in amyloid plaque formation, have shown promise in clinical trials, though they have been limited by side effects and insufficient efficacy in slowing cognitive decline. This is the first study where multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD) was employed to identify potential synergistic inhibitor combinations from among thousands of small molecules that could yield better results than the current phase-III inhibitors of BACE1. The recent phase III drugs such as Atabecestat, Elenbecestat, Lanabecestat, and Verubecestat were considered to be standards for comparison in this study. A library of small molecules with known IC50 values against BACE1 was filtered for flagging Pan-Assay Interference (PAINS) and "Brenk" compounds. Single-ligand docking revealed individual ligand interactions with the protein, forming the basis for creating ligand pairs tested in MLSD. Among these combinations, CHEMBL4078427 and CHEMBL3656158, CHEMBL4078427 and CHEMBL3695732, Verubecestat and CHEMBL3656158, and CHEMBL4078427 and Lanabecestat demonstrated excellent binding affinity of -19.90 kcal/mol, -18.45 kcal/mol, -18.07 kcal/mol, and -17.67 kcal/mol with the protein, which is significantly greater than those of phase-III inhibitors, along with inter-ligand interactions indicative of a synergistic effect. These findings underscore the transformative potential of MLSD in identifying synergistic compound interactions, paving the way for novel combination therapies in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

AI.tldr: This study applies multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD) for the first time to identify synergistic inhibitor combinations against BACE1 for Alzheimer's disease, screening thousands of small molecules against phase-III inhibitors as benchmarks. Four ligand pairs demonstrated significantly better binding affinities than current phase-III inhibitors, suggesting promising avenues for combination therapies.
AI.motivation: Current BACE1 inhibitors for Alzheimer's disease (phase-III drugs such as Atabecestat, Elenbecestat, Lanabecestat, and Verubecestat) have shown limited efficacy and undesirable side effects, failing to adequately slow cognitive decline. Therefore, there is a pressing need to discover more effective therapeutic approaches for this progressive neurodegenerative disorder.
AI.method: The study employed multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD) to screen a library of small molecules with known IC50 values against BACE1. Compounds were filtered to exclude Pan-Assay Interference (PAINS) and "Brenk" flagged compounds. Single-ligand docking was first performed to establish individual ligand-protein interactions, which formed the basis for creating ligand pairs subsequently tested via MLSD. Results were compared against four phase-III BACE1 inhibitors as standards.
AI.result: Four ligand combinations demonstrated excellent binding affinities: CHEMBL4078427+CHEMBL3656158 (-19.90 kcal/mol), CHEMBL4078427+CHEMBL3695732 (-18.45 kcal/mol), Verubecestat+CHEMBL3656158 (-18.07 kcal/mol), and CHEMBL4078427+Lanabecestat (-17.67 kcal/mol). These values significantly surpassed those of phase-III inhibitors alone, with detected inter-ligand interactions indicating synergistic effects.
AI.conclusion: MLSD holds transformative potential for identifying synergistic compound interactions that outperform current single-agent BACE1 inhibitors. The identified ligand pairs pave the way for novel combination therapies in Alzheimer's disease treatment.

title: A Roadmap for MEG Foundation Models
summary: Foundation models are beginning to reshape brain-signal analysis by moving the field beyond task-specific decoding pipelines toward reusable models pretrained on broad neural datasets. Magnetoencephalography (MEG) is a compelling but still underdeveloped target for this shift: it captures human cortical dynamics at millisecond resolution while offering stronger spatial interpretability than EEG, making it especially valuable for source-resolved studies of perception, language, cognition, and clinical brain function. Yet MEG foundation models remain at an early stage, with only a small number of MEG-specific and MEG-inclusive multi-modal models, modest pretraining corpora, and emerging but still limited benchmarks. This perspective lays down the basic concepts needed to understand MEG foundation models and provides a didactic overview of the field's key design choices, including tokenization, sensor- versus source-space representations, sensor-geometry encoding, backbone architectures, self-supervised objectives, and pretraining data. We then offer a roadmap for future development, organized around native MEG pretraining, adaptation of EEG foundation models, transfer from generic time-series models, and multi-modal integration with EEG, fMRI, MRI, behaviour, and stimulus features. We highlight the need for coordinated infrastructure, including diverse and reusable MEG datasets, rigorous evaluation across subjects, sites, tasks, and clinical settings, and responsible data-sharing practices that address consent, privacy, access, and governance.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper provides a foundational overview of MEG foundation models, covering key design choices (tokenization, sensor/source space, geometry encoding, architectures, objectives, data) and offering a development roadmap spanning native MEG pretraining, EEG foundation model adaptation, time-series transfer, and multi-modal integration, while emphasizing the need for coordinated infrastructure and responsible data practices.
AI.motivation: MEG is a compelling modality for brain-signal foundation models due to its millisecond temporal resolution and superior spatial interpretability over EEG, yet MEG foundation models remain underdeveloped with few models, modest pretraining corpora, and limited benchmarks. The authors aim to establish basic concepts and clarify design choices to accelerate progress in this emerging field.
AI.method: The paper takes a perspective/high-level review approach: it systematically lays out the conceptual foundations of MEG foundation models, provides a didactic overview of design choices (tokenization, sensor- vs source-space, sensor-geometry encoding, backbone architectures, self-supervised objectives, pretraining data), and proposes a future roadmap organized around four development paths (native MEG pretraining, EEG FM adaptation, generic time-series transfer, and multi-modal integration with EEG, fMRI, MRI, behavior, and stimuli).
AI.result: The paper identifies the current limitations of MEG foundation models, systematically categorizes their key design decisions, and outlines concrete future directions and infrastructure requirements, including the need for diverse reusable datasets, rigorous cross-subject/site/task/clinical evaluation, and responsible data governance.
AI.conclusion: Advancing MEG foundation models requires coordinated community effort on infrastructure, standardized evaluation, and data-sharing ethics, alongside continued methodological development across pretraining strategies and multi-modal integration to fully realize MEG's potential for brain-signal research.

title: The physical foundation beneath protein generative modeling
summary: Physical equations in protein modeling appear to have been replaced by generative models trained directly on structure data. By learning a mapping from noise to data, sampling de novo protein structures has become much more efficient. However, such models can also learn non-physical features and break down with out-of-distribution settings which are typical in protein design campaigns. In this review, we highlight where the physics persists in protein generative modeling pipelines and the issues that linger when physically relevant components of a macromolecular system are left unmodeled. We present a perspective that respecting the underlying physics of macromolecular systems, increasingly through learned representations that are physically grounded and updating generative models with experimental data, is foundational to generative modeling for functional protein design.

AI.tldr: This review examines the role of physics in protein generative modeling, arguing that while diffusion-based generative models have replaced physical equations for de novo protein structure sampling, they can learn non-physical features and fail in out-of-distribution settings. The authors advocate for physically grounded learned representations and integrating experimental data into generative models as foundational for functional protein design.
AI.motivation: Physical equations in protein modeling have been largely replaced by generative models trained on structure data. While these models are more efficient for de novo sampling, they can learn non-physical features and break down in out-of-distribution settings typical of protein design campaigns. This motivates a review of where physics persists in these pipelines and what issues arise when physical components are unmodeled.
AI.method: This is a perspective/review paper that surveys protein generative modeling pipelines, highlighting where physics remains embedded in the workflow, and identifying problems caused by neglecting physically relevant components of macromolecular systems. It presents a viewpoint advocating for physically grounded learned representations and updating generative models with experimental data.
AI.result: The review identifies that while generative models have made de novo protein structure sampling highly efficient, they risk learning non-physical features and failing in out-of-distribution contexts. It highlights lingering issues when physical components of macromolecular systems are left unmodeled and argues that physically grounded representations combined with experimental data integration are foundational for functional protein design.
AI.conclusion: Respecting underlying physics through physically grounded learned representations and incorporating experimental data into generative models is essential for achieving robust, functional protein design, especially in out-of-distribution scenarios.

title: When Quantization Breaks Memory: Recurrent-State Write-Back in Low-Precision Temporal Inference
summary: Quantization is widely used to reduce the computational and memory demands of neural-network inference. In recurrent networks, however, the quantized state is stored and returned at the next time step, so the rule used to store that state can alter subsequent computations. Here, we introduce recurrent-state write-back to denote this rule and isolate its effect in a compact GRU encoder--decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging, a molecular imaging modality used in quantitative biological imaging. A central task is estimating two lifetime parameters, the short-lived component τ1 and the long-lived component τ2, from high-noise time-resolved fluorescence signals. Holding the trained model fixed, replacing continuous state propagation with deterministic 4-bit state storage increases estimation errors for τ1 and τ2 by approximately 70x and 300x, respectively. Failure occurs when repeated small updates remain below the write threshold, leaving the stored state nearly fixed while the network continues to propose change. Error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory carry information from these suppressed updates across time and recover accuracy without retraining. Precision sweeps show that increasing state precision can worsen a fixed recurrent solution, while matched training shows that compatibility with the state interface can be learned. To test whether this behavior extends beyond the GRU, we repeat the post-training intervention in an independently trained LSTM, where coarse write-back reproduces the failure, error feedback restores accuracy, and state-specific interventions reveal greater sensitivity of the cell state than the hidden state. Our results establish recurrent-state write-back as a key determinant of low-precision recurrent dynamics and identify the state-storage interface as a central design consideration for quantized recurrent inference.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the concept of "recurrent-state write-back" — the rule governing how quantized recurrent states are stored and returned at subsequent time steps — and demonstrates its critical impact on low-precision recurrent neural network inference. Using a compact GRU encoder-decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging, the authors show that deterministic 4-bit state storage (vs. continuous propagation) increases estimation errors for τ1 and τ2 by ~70x and ~300x respectively. They identify the failure mechanism (suppressed small updates below the write threshold) and recover accuracy without retraining via error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory. The findings generalize to LSTM architectures and establish state-storage interface design as central to quantized recurrent inference.
AI.motivation: While quantization is widely used to reduce computational/memory costs in neural networks, its effect on recurrent networks is unique because the quantized state is stored and fed back at the next time step. This means the rule for storing the state (write-back) can alter subsequent computations. The authors aim to isolate and characterize this understudied effect, particularly in the context of fluorescence lifetime imaging where high-noise signals require precise estimation of two lifetime parameters.
AI.method: The authors introduce the concept of recurrent-state write-back and isolate its effect in a compact GRU encoder-decoder for fluorescence lifetime imaging. They hold the trained model fixed and compare continuous state propagation vs. deterministic 4-bit state storage. They then apply post-training interventions (error feedback, residual memory, direction memory) to recover accuracy without retraining, conduct precision sweeps, compare with matched training at the quantized state interface, and validate findings on an independently trained LSTM with state-specific interventions (cell vs. hidden state).
AI.result: Deterministic 4-bit state write-back vs. continuous propagation increases estimation errors by ~70x (τ1) and ~300x (τ2). Failure occurs when small repeated updates fall below the write threshold, leaving stored state nearly fixed while the network continues proposing change. Error feedback, residual memory, and direction memory recover accuracy without retraining. Increasing state precision can worsen a fixed recurrent solution, while matched training learns compatibility with the state interface. The failure pattern reproduces in an independently trained LSTM, where the cell state shows greater sensitivity than the hidden state.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent-state write-back is a key determinant of low-precision recurrent dynamics. The state-storage interface should be considered a central design consideration for quantized recurrent inference — affecting both accuracy and how precision sweeps perform. Post-hoc interventions (error feedback, residual memory, direction memory) offer effective recovery strategies without retraining.

title: A Semantic Model of Genetic Evidence: A Step Toward Bridging the Basic-Science-Clinic Gap
comment: 16 pages; supplementary material (32 pages) included in this submission. Schema, annotations, and code: https://github.com/ForomePlatform/genetic-evidence-model (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22260686)
summary: Scientific and clinical decision-making depends on evidence from the primary literature, but existing standards for representing that evidence (FHIR Evidence, ECO, SEPIO, and the GA4GH Genomic Knowledge Standards) are oriented toward clinical-trial workflows, evidence codes, or single-variant assertions, and do not capture the fine-grained, domain-specific structure of claims in basic and pre-clinical research. We introduce a semantic model for scientific evidence with three core classes, specialize it for genetics, align it structurally to FHIR Evidence with a SEPIO-anchored credibility decomposition, and attach a compact dimensional vocabulary whose conditional-activation rules are validated by a SHACL schema for the implemented constraints. Using clinical variant interpretation as the driving use case, we evaluate the model through a human-AI annotation pilot over six genetics papers, yielding 28 evidence items and 95 source-anchored assertions, with a workflow that keeps curator-authored reference annotations distinct from AI-drafted annotations. Treating the pilot as a feasibility study rather than a benchmark, we argue that the model is a useful increment toward trustworthy, AI-ready infrastructure for variant interpretation: a reference data model and validation schema for representing genetic evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a semantic model for representing fine-grained, domain-specific claims in basic and pre-clinical genetic research, structurally aligned to FHIR Evidence with a SEPIO-anchored credibility decomposition and validated by a SHACL schema. A human-AI annotation pilot over six genetics papers produced 28 evidence items and 95 source-anchored assertions, demonstrating the model as a feasible step toward AI-ready infrastructure for variant interpretation.
AI.motivation: Existing standards for representing scientific evidence (FHIR Evidence, ECO, SEPIO, GA4GH) are oriented toward clinical-trial workflows, evidence codes, or single-variant assertions and fail to capture the fine-grained, domain-specific structure of claims in basic and pre-clinical research.
AI.method: The authors propose a semantic model with three core classes, specialized for genetics, aligned structurally to FHIR Evidence with a SEPIO-anchored credibility decomposition, and validated via a SHACL schema with a compact dimensional vocabulary employing conditional-activation rules. They evaluate through a human-AI annotation pilot over six genetics papers, keeping curator-authored reference annotations distinct from AI-drafted annotations.
AI.result: The pilot yielded 28 evidence items and 95 source-anchored assertions across six genetics papers, treated as a feasibility study rather than a benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The model represents a useful increment toward trustworthy, AI-ready infrastructure for variant interpretation by providing a reference data model and validation schema for representing genetic evidence.

title: Stochastic epidemic models with pulse vaccination, varying infectivity and waning immunity
summary: We introduce a fully stochastic, non-Markovian SIRS-type epidemic model that incorporates varying infectivity, waning immunity and a pulse vaccination strategy that may not confer permanent immunity. The model is constructed at the individual level, where each person is characterized by random infectivity and susceptibility functions, and vaccination campaigns occur at the jump times of a Poisson random measure with arbitrary intensity. We rigorously derive the epidemic dynamics as the large-population limit of an interacting stochastic particle system, leading to a system of nonlinear Volterra-type integral equations governing the average susceptibility and total force of infection. We establish a functional law of large numbers(FLLN) for the empirical processes and provide explicit expressions for the limiting compartmental proportions. The long-term behavior of the system is analyzed: we prove that the infection-free solution is globally asymptotically stable when the basic reproduction number falls below a critical threshold, and that the disease persists when this threshold is exceeded. The threshold is given by the harmonic mean of the maximal susceptibility across individuals and generalizes previous results by incorporating vaccination and memory effects. Our framework provides a probabilistically grounded extension of classical deterministic pulse vaccination models and offers new insights into the control of epidemics through scheduled immunization policies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a fully stochastic, non-Markovian SIRS-type epidemic model with varying infectivity, waning immunity, and pulse vaccination. The authors derive large-population limits of an interacting particle system, establishing a functional law of large numbers leading to nonlinear Volterra integral equations. They prove global stability of the infection-free state below a critical basic reproduction number threshold (given by a harmonic mean of maximal susceptibility) and disease persistence above it, generalizing classical deterministic pulse vaccination models.
AI.motivation: To extend classical deterministic pulse vaccination epidemic models to a probabilistically rigorous, individual-level stochastic framework that captures realistic features such as variable infectivity, non-permanent immunity, and waning immunity, while providing mathematical guarantees on long-term epidemic behavior and threshold conditions.
AI.method: The model is built at the individual level with random infectivity and susceptibility functions. Vaccination occurs at jump times of a Poisson random measure with arbitrary intensity. The authors rigorously derive the large-population limit of the interacting stochastic particle system, yielding a system of nonlinear Volterra-type integral equations. They establish a functional law of large numbers for the empirical processes and analyze long-term stability via a basic reproduction number threshold expressed as a harmonic mean of maximal susceptibility.
AI.result: Explicit limiting compartmental proportions are obtained from the FLLN. The infection-free solution is shown to be globally asymptotically stable when the basic reproduction number is below a critical threshold, while disease persists when the threshold is exceeded. The threshold generalizes earlier results by incorporating vaccination and memory effects.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a probabilistically grounded generalization of classical deterministic pulse vaccination SIRS models and offers new insights into epidemic control through scheduled immunization policies.

title: VizIt: A multi-view framework for exploring single-cell, spatial, and genetic data online
summary: Multi-omic studies increasingly require data to be examined from complementary biological perspectives, yet interactive exploration remains fragmented across modalities and tools. We present VizIt, an open-source framework for multi-view exploration of single-cell and spatial transcriptomic, epigenomic and genetic data. VizIt connects gene-, cell type-, condition-, spatial-, genomic region- and variant-centered views, enabling seamless navigation across biological perspectives. We demonstrate VizIt through the Parkinson's Cell Atlas, a customizable interactive multi-omic resource.

AI.tldr: VizIt is an open-source framework for multi-view exploration of single-cell and spatial multi-omic data, connecting gene-, cell type-, condition-, spatial-, genomic region-, and variant-centered views, demonstrated through the Parkinson's Cell Atlas.
AI.motivation: Multi-omic studies require examination from complementary biological perspectives, but interactive exploration is fragmented across different modalities and tools, creating a need for unified multi-view exploration.
AI.method: VizIt provides an open-source framework that links multiple biological perspectives — including gene, cell type, condition, spatial, genomic region, and variant-centered views — to enable seamless navigation across data modalities such as single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, epigenomics, and genetics.
AI.result: The framework is demonstrated through the Parkinson's Cell Atlas, a customizable interactive multi-omic resource built with VizIt.
AI.conclusion: VizIt addresses the fragmentation of interactive multi-omic data exploration by providing an integrated multi-view framework, validated via its application to the Parkinson's Cell Atlas.

title: Simulation-free Unbalanced Dynamic Optimal Transport with General Growth Penalty
summary: Inferring cellular dynamics from unpaired single-cell snapshots requires modeling both state transitions and population growth or death. Unbalanced dynamic optimal transport (UDOT) addresses this by penalizing growth along transport paths, making the choice of growth penalty a key way to encode biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis. However, existing UDOT solvers either rely on computationally expensive NeuralODE simulations or depend on analytical solutions of conditional paths, restricting their efficiency solely to quadratic penalties, i.e. Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao (WFR) geodesics. To enable an efficient UDOT solver for general growth penalties, we first show that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport are separated. We then introduce \textbf{S}imulation-free \textbf{U}nbalanced \textbf{D}ynamic \textbf{O}ptimal transport (SUDO), a simulation-free framework for UDOT with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties. SUDO learns the conditional paths and transport costs, solves the induced semi-coupling problem, and subsequently leverages unbalanced flow matching to achieve a simulation-free solution. On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of efficient, analytical solution-driven algorithms while outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR, SUDO supports asymmetric penalties that encode proliferation-dominant priors and produce more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.

AI.tldr: SUDO is a simulation-free framework for unbalanced dynamic optimal transport (UDOT) that supports general non-quadratic convex growth penalties, achieving efficient solutions while matching the accuracy of analytical WFR-based methods and outperforming simulation-based approaches in speed and biological plausibility.
AI.motivation: Existing UDOT solvers are either computationally expensive (NeuralODE simulations) or restricted to quadratic penalties (WFR geodesics) due to reliance on analytical solutions. There is a need for an efficient UDOT solver that supports general growth penalties to better encode biological priors on proliferation and apoptosis.
AI.method: SUDO first shows that concave growth penalties lead to degenerate solutions where growth and transport are separated. It then learns conditional paths and transport costs, solves the induced semi-coupling problem, and leverages unbalanced flow matching to achieve a simulation-free solution for UDOT with general non-quadratic convex growth penalties.
AI.result: On WFR benchmarks, SUDO matches the accuracy of analytical solution-driven algorithms while outperforming simulation-based methods in computational speed. Beyond WFR, SUDO supports asymmetric penalties encoding proliferation-dominant priors, producing more plausible trajectories and growth estimates on synthetic and single-cell datasets.
AI.conclusion: SUDO provides an efficient, simulation-free approach to UDOT that generalizes beyond quadratic penalties, enabling flexible encoding of biological priors and yielding more realistic cellular dynamics inference from single-cell snapshots.

title: Eco-evolutionary cycles in a matching type predator-prey interaction
summary: We study the population dynamics of a predator-prey system with two types in each species. Within a species, predator or prey, dynamics are described by a neutral competitive Lotka-Volterra model, i.e., birth, death and competition parameters are equal for both types. Additionally, we assume that the intra- and inter-type competition parameters are equal. The predator-prey interaction is defined by a matching-types model where predators of type $i$ exclusively interact with prey of type $i$. The individual-based model is described by a birth-death process with immigration, where immigration reflects mutations between the types of the same species. We completely describe the deterministic dynamics arising as a large population limit of this birth-death process. We find that depending on the parameters, potential equilibria are the coexistence of all four types, coexistence of a non-matching or matching pair of predators and prey, or the extinction of the predator or prey species resulting in a line of two-type equilibria. When mutations are sufficiently rare, then the predator-prey dynamics are described by successive jumps between the different deterministic equilibria on this mutational time scale. These jumps describe eco-evolutionary cycles of repeated prey or predator invasions and declines. When coexistence of all the types is possible, we show that these cycles accumulate on this time scale. Lastly, to prove that after the accumulation point the system converges to the coexistence equilibrium, we consider a slightly modified model with unequal intra- and inter-type competition parameters. This modified setting allows us to conclude that after the accumulation point all four populations remain macroscopic and converge to the coexistence equilibrium.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a predator-prey system with two types per species under neutral competition and matching-type interactions. It derives the deterministic large-population limit and shows that with rare mutations, eco-evolutionary cycles of repeated predator/prey invasions and declines emerge on the mutational timescale. When coexistence of all types is possible, these cycles accumulate, and the system subsequently converges to the coexistence equilibrium.
AI.motivation: To understand how rare mutations and neutral within-species dynamics interact with predator-prey matching-type interactions to produce eco-evolutionary dynamics, and to fully characterize the resulting deterministic equilibria and long-term evolutionary behavior.
AI.method: The individual-based model is formulated as a birth-death process with immigration (representing mutation). The authors analyze the deterministic large-population limit, characterize all potential equilibria, and study the system on the mutational timescale to describe jumps between equilibria. A modified model with unequal intra- and inter-type competition is introduced to prove convergence after the accumulation point.
AI.result: Possible equilibria include coexistence of all four types, coexistence of matching or non-matching predator-prey pairs, or extinction of one species leading to a line of two-type equilibria. Rare mutations yield successive jumps between equilibria, generating eco-evolutionary cycles. When all-type coexistence is possible, these cycles accumulate, after which the system converges to the coexistence equilibrium (proven via the modified competition model).
AI.conclusion: The study provides a complete characterization of deterministic equilibria in this neutral predator-prey system and demonstrates that rare mutations drive punctuated eco-evolutionary cycles, with a well-defined accumulation point leading to coexistence of all four types.

title: A Short Combinatorial Proof of the Pons-Batle Identity for Counting Tree-Child Networks
summary: Tree-child networks are a useful class of binary phylogenetic networks. The Pons--Batle identity (Pons and Batle, \textit{Scientific Reports}, 2021) states that the number $a_{n,k}$ of tree-child networks with $k$ reticulations on $n$ taxa satisfies \[ a_{n,k}=(n-k+1)a_{n,k-1} +\frac{n(2n+k-3)}{n-k}a_{n-1,k}. \] In this paper, we present a short combinatorial proof of this identity.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a short combinatorial proof of the Pons-Batle identity, which counts tree-child networks with k reticulations on n taxa, without relying on algebraic or generating function methods.
AI.motivation: The Pons-Batle identity is an important recurrence for counting tree-child networks, but its original proof was likely algebraic in nature. A purely combinatorial proof would provide deeper structural insight into why this identity holds.
AI.method: The authors present a bijective or counting-based argument that interprets each term in the recurrence in terms of structural features of tree-child networks, showing that removing or modifying reticulation nodes and taxa accounts for the two terms in the identity.
AI.result: A concise combinatorial derivation of the Pons-Batle identity is obtained, offering an alternative to previous non-combinatorial proofs.
AI.conclusion: The combinatorial proof sheds new light on the structure of tree-child networks and validates the Pons-Batle recurrence from a purely enumerative perspective.

title: Layered mixed matrices and reaction networks
summary:
The purpose of this work is twofold. In the first part, we consider layered mixed matrices introduced by Murota, relate them to existing notions in combinatorial commutative algebra, and investigate the irreducibility of their determinants. Furthermore, for a layered mixed matrix in combinatorial canonical form, we determine the sparsity structure of its inverse. That is, we characterize which entries of the inverse are nonzero.
  In the second part, we establish for the first time a formal connection between these algebraic results and the theory of buffering structures for reaction networks developed by Mochizuki and Okada. We identify the lattice of buffering structures with the lattice of order ideals of the block poset of the combinatorial canonical form of the associated layered mixed matrix. This allows us to characterize the reducibility of the symbolic Jacobian determinant as a polynomial in the reaction-rate derivatives, as well as the nonzero sensitivity responses of species concentrations to reaction-rate perturbations.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges combinatorial commutative algebra and reaction network theory by analyzing layered mixed matrices, their determinant irreducibility, and inverse sparsity structure, then formally connecting these algebraic results to Mochizuki-Okada's buffering structures via a lattice isomorphism between buffering structures and order ideals of a block poset.
AI.motivation: The work aims to connect two seemingly disparate areas: (1) algebraic properties of layered mixed matrices (determinant irreducibility and inverse sparsity) and (2) buffering structures in reaction networks—establishing a formal mathematical bridge between them to characterize sensitivity and reducibility properties of reaction networks.
AI.method: The paper proceeds in two parts. First, it studies layered mixed matrices introduced by Murota, relating them to notions in combinatorial commutative algebra and analyzing determinant irreducibility and inverse sparsity structure via the combinatorial canonical form. Second, it establishes a lattice isomorphism between buffering structures of reaction networks and order ideals of the block poset of the combinatorial canonical form of the associated layered mixed matrix.
AI.result: The paper determines which entries of the inverse of a layered mixed matrix in combinatorial canonical form are nonzero, and identifies the lattice of buffering structures with the lattice of order ideals of the block poset. This yields characterizations of symbolic Jacobian determinant reducibility as a polynomial in reaction-rate derivatives and of nonzero sensitivity responses of species concentrations to reaction-rate perturbations.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully establishes the first formal connection between layered mixed matrix theory (from combinatorial algebra) and buffering structure theory (from reaction network biology), providing algebraic tools to characterize sensitivity and reducibility in reaction networks.

title: Quantum Optimisation for Protein-Protein Interaction Network Alignment
summary: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network alignment combines topological and sequence information to identify conserved modules across species, but global alignment remains challenging: heuristics sacrifice optimality, while exact methods lack scalability. We model the alignment as a weighted maximum common induced subgraph problem and reformulate it through the modular product graph to a minimum-weight vertex cover on the complement, with node weights carrying sequence similarity. To solve this problem, we develop a hybrid framework combining kernelisation, branch-and-bound, and seven Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) formulations. These formulations differ in how the cover constraints are enforced, from penalty terms in the cost Hamiltonian to mixers confined to the feasible subspace. For single round QAOA, we derive closed-form expressions for the expected cost of four circulant mixer variants, enabling performance characterisation without circuit simulation. Applied to synthetic and real-world networks reduced to KEGG pathways, the QAOA formulations achieve high topological conservation on the aligned core while at least maintaining biological conservation comparable to leading classical aligners, at the cost of reduced node coverage. Across selected KEGG pathways, the aligned subnetworks retain disease-associated proteins, preserving biologically relevant information. Cheaper formulations leave more edges uncovered, while enforcing feasibility in the mixer raises circuit depth by one to two orders of magnitude. Together, these results highlight the potential of quantum optimisation for PPI network alignment and the resource trade-offs that will shape its scalability as quantum hardware matures.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical framework for global PPI network alignment, reformulating it as a minimum-weight vertex cover problem solved via kernelisation, branch-and-bound, and seven QAOA variants with different constraint enforcement strategies.
AI.motivation: Global PPI network alignment is challenging because heuristic methods sacrifice optimality while exact methods fail to scale. This motivates developing an alternative approach that can achieve both quality and scalability.
AI.method: The alignment is modeled as a weighted maximum common induced subgraph problem, reformulated via the modular product graph into a minimum-weight vertex cover on the complement. A hybrid solver combines kernelisation, branch-and-bound, and seven QAOA formulations differing in how cover constraints are enforced (from penalty terms in the cost Hamiltonian to mixers confined to the feasible subspace). Closed-form expressions are derived for the expected cost of four circulant mixer variants in single-round QAOA.
AI.result: On synthetic and real KEGG pathway networks, QAOA formulations achieve high topological conservation on the aligned core and maintain biological conservation comparable to leading classical aligners, though with reduced node coverage. Aligned subnetworks retain disease-associated proteins. Cheaper formulations leave more edges uncovered, while feasibility-enforcing mixers increase circuit depth by one to two orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Quantum optimisation shows promise for PPI network alignment, but there are significant trade-offs between formulation cost, circuit depth, and node coverage that will shape scalability as quantum hardware matures.

title: A Generalizable Feature Extractor for Alzheimer's-Related Brain MRI Tasks
comment: 26 pages (excluding the references section), 7 figures (excluding sub-figures)
summary: When there is not enough labeled data to properly train deep learning models, transfer learning can help. We still do not fully understand how effective it is in neuroimaging, especially for Alzheimer's disease research. It is also not clear if these transferred models can work on new datasets without being retrained for each specific task. We evaluate whether a compact, supervised pretrained model can serve as a reusable foundation model for downstream neuroimaging tasks. We freeze the 7.18 million weights of a 3D CNN previously trained for brain-age prediction, and adapt it to each task using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), requiring only ~1% additional trainable parameters. We evaluate generalizability in six experiments. Adapting the model to classify cognitively normal versus Dementia on ADNI gave an AUC of 0.964 on held-out folds (Experiment #1). Applying that adapted model unchanged to OASIS-3, with no retraining, gave an AUC of 0.871 (Experiment #2). Reusing its output logit together with age and a cognitive score distinguished stable from progressing MCI with an AUC of 0.828 (Experiment #3). Adapting the same backbone to predict amyloid positivity from structural MRI gave an AUC of 0.804 (Experiment #4). Finally, the same approach estimated ICV-normalized hippocampal and white matter hypointensity volumes directly from the T1w image, with R^2 of 0.80 and 0.91 respectively, tasks normally addressed with much larger U-Net networks (Experiments #5 and #6). A compact model supervised on brain age can therefore serve as a reusable backbone, adapting to each task with ~1% additional parameters and transferring to an unseen cohort without any training. Our findings suggest that a carefully trained brain age model can serve as an effective foundation model for Alzheimer's related tasks, even under strict data constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether a compact, supervised 3D CNN pretrained for brain-age prediction can serve as a reusable foundation model for downstream Alzheimer's disease neuroimaging tasks. By freezing the 7.18M weights and using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with only ~1% additional trainable parameters, the model successfully adapts to six tasks including dementia classification (AUC 0.964 on ADNI, 0.871 on unseen OASIS-3 cohort), MCI progression prediction (AUC 0.828), amyloid positivity prediction (AUC 0.804), and volumetric regression tasks (R² of 0.80-0.91), demonstrating that a brain-age model can effectively serve as a foundation model under strict data constraints.
AI.motivation: There is insufficient labeled data to properly train deep learning models for Alzheimer's disease research, and the effectiveness of transfer learning in neuroimaging remains poorly understood. It is unclear whether pretrained models can generalize to new datasets without task-specific retraining.
AI.method: The authors freeze the 7.18 million weights of a 3D CNN previously trained for brain-age prediction and adapt it to each downstream task using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), requiring only ~1% additional trainable parameters. Six experiments evaluate generalizability across classification and regression tasks on different datasets.
AI.result: The adapted model achieved AUC of 0.964 for dementia classification on ADNI, transferred with no retraining to OASIS-3 at AUC 0.871, distinguished stable from progressing MCI at AUC 0.828, predicted amyloid positivity at AUC 0.804, and estimated hippocampal and white matter hypointensity volumes with R² of 0.80 and 0.91 respectively—tasks typically requiring much larger U-Net architectures.
AI.conclusion: A compact, carefully trained brain-age model can serve as an effective foundation model for Alzheimer's-related tasks, transferring to unseen cohorts without retraining and adapting efficiently with minimal additional parameters, even under strict data constraints.
